title: Modules, free modules, and annihilators
terms: module; submodule; module homomorphism; free module; torsion module; torsion-free module; annihilator.

exposition.text:
A module over a ring with identity generalizes a vector space: it has an abelian addition law
and scalar multiplication satisfying distributivity, associativity, and the identity axiom. Scalars
need not have inverses. Modules over a field are vector spaces, while modules over Z are abelian
groups. A submodule is closed under addition and scalar multiplication; a module homomor-
phism preserves both. A free module has a basis with unique finite scalar expressions.
Over an integral domain, a torsion element is killed by some nonzero scalar, a module is a tor-
sion module when every element is torsion, and it is torsion-free when only zero is torsion. The
annihilator of an element m is the ideal {r : rm = 0}. Torsion-free does not imply free over an
arbitrary domain, though a finitely generated torsion-free module over a principal ideal domain
is free. Quotient modules can be studied through the relations imposed on generators.

question.text:
For the Z-module M = (Z/12Z) ⊕ (Z/18Z), what is the annihilator ideal of m = (2, 3)?
(A) 2Z (B) 3Z (C) 6Z (D) 12Z (E) 36Z

solution.text:
The condition km = 0 requires 12 | 2k and 18 | 3k. Both are equivalent to 6 | k. Thus the
annihilator is exactly 6Z, not the ideal determined by the orders of the entire summands.

question.text:
As a module over Z, the additive group Q is
(A) free of rank one.
(B) a nonzero torsion module.
(C) torsion-free but not free.
(D) free of rank two.
(E) neither torsion-free nor divisible.

solution.text:
If a nonzero integer kills a rational number, that number is zero, so Q is torsion-free. Every
rational number is divisible by two within Q. In a nonzero free Z-module, a basis vector
cannot equal twice another vector, because its coefficient one would have to be twice an in-
teger. Thus Q is not free. It is not finitely generated, so the finitely generated PID theorem
is not contradicted.

Thus the listed vectors span M and are independent over Z. The ambient standard basis is
not contained in M, while the two even coordinate vectors fail to generate (1, 1).
